title: At the restaurant, at the pharmacy, and in an emergency
title_target: 我不舒服 — Wǒ bù shūfu
goal: Order food from start to paying the bill, say which part of your body hurts, ask for help — and pull together every sentence frame from all twelve units in the most demanding situations.
bekal: order food and drinks at a restaurant
say what hurts with the 我…疼 pattern
ask for help in an emergency

dialogs.title: 对话 1 — Ordering food
dialogs.intro: Andi and Wang Li at a Sichuan restaurant. This is a conversation you'll repeat hundreds of times; memorize the frame, not the words.

lines.speaker: 服务员:
lines.id: How many?

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: Two. Do you have a table by the window?

lines.speaker: 服务员:
lines.id: Yes, please follow me. Here's the menu.
lines.literal: have, please — with — me — come. this — be — dish-list.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Thanks. What's best here?
lines.literal: thank. you-all — here — what — most — good-to-eat.

lines.speaker: 服务员:
lines.text: [水煮鱼|Shuǐzhǔ yú][和|hé][宫保鸡丁|gōngbǎo jīdīng][最|zuì][有名|yǒumíng]。
lines.id: The spicy boiled fish and the kung pao chicken are the most famous.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Is the boiled fish spicy? I can't really handle spicy food.
lines.literal: water-boil-fish — spicy — (question). I — not — too — able — eat — spicy.

lines.speaker: 服务员:
lines.id: Very spicy. We can make it mild.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [那|Nà][来|lái][一|yí][个|ge][微辣|wēi là][的|de][水煮鱼|shuǐzhǔ yú]。[还有|Háiyǒu]，[我|wǒ][不|bù][吃|chī][猪肉|zhūròu]。
lines.id: Then one mild boiled fish. Oh, and I don't eat pork.
lines.literal: that — come — one — (classifier) — slight — spicy — (one) — water-boil-fish. also, I — not — eat — pig-meat.

lines.speaker: 服务员:
lines.id: Got it. Anything else?

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.text: [再|Zài][来|lái][一|yí][个|ge][青菜|qīngcài]、[两|liǎng][碗|wǎn][米饭|mǐfàn][和|hé][一|yì][壶|hú][茶|chá]。
lines.id: Plus a plate of greens, two bowls of rice and a pot of tea.
lines.literal: again — come — one — (classifier) — green-vegetable, two — bowl — rice — and — one — pot — tea.

lines.speaker: 服务员:
lines.id: Sure, just a moment, please.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Excuse me, the check, please!

notes: **[位|wèi] is the polite classifier for people.** Servers always use it: [几位|jǐ wèi]？ how many? You answer with number + 位 too: [两位|liǎng wèi].

**⚠️ To order food, use [来|lái] "come", not 要 or 买.** [来一个水煮鱼|Lái yí ge shuǐzhǔ yú] = one boiled fish. It sounds odd translated literally, but it's what people say. [要|yào] works too and is just as correct; 买 is never used at the table.
**[再来一个…|Zài lái yí ge…] = "one more …".** 再 before a verb means "again, once more" — and it's used for things that **haven't** happened yet. For things that already happened, use [又|yòu].
**[微辣|wēi là] mild · [中辣|zhōng là] medium · [特辣|tè là] extra hot · [不辣|bú là] not spicy.** These four words will save your dinner in Sichuan or Hunan.

**⚠️ [我不吃猪肉|Wǒ bù chī zhūròu] is a must-memorize sentence** for Muslim travelers. Say it before you order, not after the food arrives. Chinese restaurants are used to hearing it and won't ask further.
**[买单|mǎidān] = the check, please**, literally "buy the bill". The synonym is [结账|jiézhàng]. Just say it with a raised hand; calling out to staff in a Chinese restaurant is normal, not rude.
**[请稍等|Qǐng shāo děng] = just a moment, please.** More polite than [等一下|děng yíxià]; you'll hear it wherever there's customer service.

head: Stage
What you say
Meaning
rows: [有中文菜单吗|Yǒu Zhōngwén càidān ma]？
Are there pictures? — a lifesaver while you can't read the characters yet
[这个是什么肉|Zhège shì shénme ròu]？
[请不要放辣椒|Qǐng bú yào fàng làjiāo]。
[我对花生过敏|Wǒ duì huāshēng guòmǐn]。
[能加点儿水吗|Néng jiā diǎnr shuǐ ma]？
Could I get this to go?

after: ⚠️ **Taking leftovers home is very common in China** and not embarrassing at all — it's seen as not being wasteful. [打包|dǎbāo] is a word you'll hear a lot.
⚠️ **Tipping isn't customary** in mainland Chinese restaurants and often just confuses the staff.

grammars.title: Food and drinks
after: ⚠️ **Chinese people rarely drink cold water.** If you just ask for water, you'll almost certainly get hot water — [热水|rè shuǐ]. If you want it cold, say so: [冰水|bīng shuǐ] or [凉水|liáng shuǐ].
⚠️ [汤|tāng] "soup" is **drunk**, not eaten: [喝汤|hē tāng]. Same with rice porridge: [喝粥|hē zhōu].

dialogs.title: 对话 2 — At the pharmacy
dialogs.intro: The next day Andi isn't feeling well. This conversation is short, but every sentence in it could genuinely save you in a foreign country.

lines.speaker: 药店:
lines.id: Hello, what do you need?

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: I don't feel well. My stomach hurts.
lines.literal: I — not — comfortable. I — stomach — hurt.

lines.speaker: 药店:
lines.id: Since when?

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [昨天|Zuótiān][晚上|wǎnshang]。[我|Wǒ][吃|chī][了|le][很|hěn][辣|là][的|de][东西|dōngxi]。
lines.id: Last night. I ate something really spicy.
lines.literal: yesterday — evening. I — eat — (done) — (prop) — spicy — (of) — thing.

lines.speaker: 药店:
lines.id: Any fever? Diarrhea?

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: No fever, but I've had diarrhea three times.
lines.literal: not-have — fever, but — pull — (done) — three — times.

lines.speaker: 药店:
lines.id: Take this medicine three times a day, after meals.
lines.literal: this — (classifier) — medicine — one — day — three — times, meal — after — eat.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: How many tablets each time?

lines.speaker: 药店:
lines.text: [两|Liǎng][片|piàn]。[多|Duō][喝|hē][热水|rè shuǐ]，[别|bié][吃|chī][辣|là][的|de]。
lines.id: Two. Drink plenty of hot water, and no spicy food.
lines.literal: two — slice. more — drink — hot-water, don't — eat — spicy — (one).

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Okay. What if it still hurts tomorrow?

lines.speaker: 药店:
lines.id: Then you'll need to go to the hospital and see a doctor.
lines.literal: that — you(polite) — must — go — hospital — see — doctor.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Got it, thank you.

notes: **⚠️ To say what hurts, use "I + body part + 疼", with no extra verb and no 的.** [我肚子疼|Wǒ dùzi téng] literally "I stomach hurt". Not 我的肚子是疼. Think of it as "me — my stomach hurts": the person first, then the part, then the pain.
**[不舒服|bù shūfu] = not feeling well.** The most useful opener when you don't yet know exactly what's wrong.
**[从什么时候开始的|Cóng shénme shíhou kāishǐ de]？** = since when. Note the 的 at the end — this is the 是…的 form from Unit 10, highlighting a detail of something that definitely happened.
**[发烧|fāshāo] fever · [咳嗽|késou] cough · [感冒|gǎnmào] cold, flu · [拉肚子|lā dùzi] diarrhea · [头晕|tóuyūn] dizzy.** Five words that cover most complaints.
**[片|piàn] is the classifier for thin, flat things**: tablets, slices of bread, pieces. [两片药|liǎng piàn yào] two tablets.

**[得|děi] = have to.** ⚠️ It's the same character as the 得 degree marker from Unit 8, but pronounced differently: *děi* (have to) and *de* (marker). Its negative isn't 不得 but [不用|bú yòng] "don't need to".
**[如果…呢|rúguǒ… ne]？ = "what if …?".** Synonym: [要是|yàoshi]. This is the simplest conditional frame, and it's all you need at A1.
**[看医生|kàn yīshēng] = see a doctor**, literally "look at a doctor". Another form: [看病|kàn bìng] "get medical treatment".

grammars.title: Body and symptoms

head: Symptom
Sentence
rows: [疼了两天了|Téng le liǎng tiān le]。

after: ⚠️ Notice that [发烧了|fāshāo le] and [感冒了|gǎnmào le] use the **change 了** from Unit 10: healthy before, not now. Without 了, the sentence sounds like you're describing a habit.

grammars.title: Emergencies

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: Help! — only when a life is in danger
[我的护照丢了|Wǒ de hùzhào diū le]。
[我的钱包被偷了|Wǒ de qiánbāo bèi tōu le]。
[我不会说中文|Wǒ bú huì shuō Zhōngwén]。
[有人会说英语吗|Yǒu rén huì shuō Yīngyǔ ma]？
[请给我叫翻译|Qǐng gěi wǒ jiào fānyì]。
[我要联系我的大使馆|Wǒ yào liánxì wǒ de dàshǐguǎn]。
I need to contact my embassy.

after: ⚠️ **Save your address in Chinese characters on your phone.** In a panic, showing it is far faster and far more reliable than trying to pronounce it.
Save your own embassy's name in Chinese too — for example, the Embassy of the Republic of Indonesia: **[印度尼西亚共和国大使馆|Yìndùníxīyà Gònghéguó Dàshǐguǎn]**. Save the Chinese name, not its translation.

The pattern
Unit

Point things out and say whose they are
[多少钱？便宜一点儿吧|Duōshao qián? Piányi yìdiǎnr ba]

Order food and ask for help
[来一个… / 我不舒服|Lái yí ge… / Wǒ bù shūfu]

blocks.title: Five rules that decide everything
items: **1. All adverbials stand before the verb.** Time, place, means, manner — all of them. Only the object, duration and number of times can come after.
**2. Adjective sentences don't use 是; they use 很.** [他很忙|Tā hěn máng], not 他是忙.
**3. A number never attaches directly to a noun.** There's always a classifier in between.
**4. 了 is not a past tense.** It marks completion or change. What marks the past is a time expression.
**5. Negation has two forms.** 不 for will and habits; 没 for events that didn't happen. 有 always takes 没有.

sections.title: Final test: a whole day in Mandarin

blocks.text: Do this in your head, out loud, without opening your notes. If you can get through the ten situations below, you've mastered this module — not just read it.

items: **07:00** You meet a neighbor in the elevator. Greet them and answer their question about how you are.
**07:30** You have breakfast at a food stall. Order two steamed buns and a soy milk, then ask the price.
**08:15** You take a taxi. Give your destination, ask how long it'll take, and ask to stop across from the bank.
**10:00** You're introduced to a new coworker. Give your name, where you're from and what you do, then ask the same.
**12:30** You have lunch together. State your dietary restrictions and order something that isn't spicy.
**14:00** You're looking for the restroom in an unfamiliar building. Ask, then repeat the directions you heard to make sure.
**16:00** Your coworker invites you to dinner. Accept, then agree on a time and place.
**18:00** You're shopping for clothes. Ask the price, ask to try it on, then bargain once.
**20:00** You talk about last weekend in six sentences, using 了 and 过.
**22:00** Your stomach hurts. Explain your symptoms at the pharmacy and ask how many times a day to take the medicine.

blocks.title: If you get stuck
items: Note which situation stopped you, then reopen that unit — not the whole module.

Stalling mid-sentence is normal even for people who've studied for years. What separates beginners from fluent speakers isn't never getting stuck, but having backup sentences: [请再说一遍|Qǐng zài shuō yí biàn]。[这个用中文怎么说|Zhège yòng Zhōngwén zěnme shuō]？
Repeat this test in a week. The difference will surprise you.
[加油|Jiāyóu]！

wave: Review the whole module: work through the "Final test" above from seven in the morning to ten at night, one situation each time you move to a different room today. Twelve units used in one day will stick far better than twelve units read in a week.
